newsitem.title: INDIA: Indian stocks rebound on tax review statement.
newsitem.headline: Indian stocks rebound on tax review statement.

text.p: India's sluggish stock markets reversed a three-week slide after Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda revived sentiment promising to review a recently introduced controversial tax on companies, brokers said on Wednesday.
The 30-share index of the Bombay Stock Exchange (BSE) was up 103.12 points, or 3.68 percent, at 2,901.69 in afternoon trade on Wednesday -- after tumbling about 33 percent since its June peak.

"Psychologically, it's a big morale booster," said Bharat Iyer, market strategist at UBS Securities, the investment arm of Union Bank of Switzerland, referring to the prime minister's statement. "It is very positive."
Deve Gowda told industrialists in New Delhi on Tuesday he would review the minimum alternate tax (MAT) on companies, which they blamed for slowing industrial growth and company profits.
"About your point on taxation, we have taken note for consideration when next year's budget is being formulated," the prime minister had said.
India's budget for fiscal 1997/98 (April-March) is normally presented to parliament in late February.
The MAT, imposed in July, hit companies that avoided paying tax by investing in tax-exempt expansions and diversifications.
Analysts said the market had been waiting for a trigger to bounce back after prices had slumped on poor first-half company results, slowing industrial production and rising fuel and energy costs.
Traders said the rebound gathered momentum as short sellers hastened to cover positions, while foreign and local funds bought selectively into the upturn.
"Bears are running for cover," said Niranjan Nandgadkar, a dealer at Arcadia Share and Stock Brokers. "There's some foreign buying too."
Foreign funds were expected to pull prices higher ahead of the year's close in order to tidy their books, traders said.
There has been an economic slowdown, but strategists are not seeing a recession.
"We feel that a turnaround over the next six months is the most probable of all scenarios," Sanjeev Mohta, research head at James Capel B&K, said in a note to investors.
"The most positive development is higher rural incomes which should drive demand growth."
UBS' Iyer was not convinced the market had bottomed out.
"In terms of valuations, the market is cheap," he said. "But there's nothing to conclude the prices won't get cheaper."
He said the government would have to take some harsh decisions such as an increase in subsidised petrol and diesel prices probably early next year.
